details:
**"Gadfly" of the state**
In Plato's Apology, Socrates compares himself to a gadfly sent by the god to sting the large, sluggish horse of Athens into wakefulness. It is the single most common clue for Socrates and his trial, explaining his habit of pestering citizens with questions.

**Trial for impiety and corrupting the youth**
In 399 BCE Socrates was charged with asebeia (impiety, including not believing in the city's gods and introducing new divinities) and with corrupting the young men of Athens. He was convicted by a jury of Athenian citizens and sentenced to death.

**Drinking hemlock and the Phaedo**
Socrates was executed by drinking a cup of poison hemlock. Plato's Phaedo depicts his last day, when he gives arguments for the immortality of the soul (including the affinity argument and recollection) before drinking the poison; as numbness spreads up from his feet, his last words are "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius."

**The Apology**
Plato's account of the defense speech Socrates gave at his trial ("apologia" means defense, not an apology). Xenophon also wrote a work with the same title about the trial. It ends with Socrates arguing that death is either a dreamless sleep ("a state of nothingness") or a journey to another place, and that only God knows whether the living or the dead are better off.

**Chaerephon and the Oracle at Delphi**
Socrates's friend Chaerephon asked the Pythian oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and was told no one was. Socrates tested this by questioning politicians, poets, and craftsmen, and concluded that he was wisest only because he knew that he knew nothing.

**Meletus, Anytus, and Lycon**
The three accusers at Socrates's trial. Meletus is the chief prosecutor whom Socrates cross-examines, asking him to name who "improves" the youth and claiming Meletus accuses him of atheism. Anytus was a prominent democratic politician, and Lycon represented the orators.

**Horses and flute-playing arguments**
In the Apology, Socrates refutes Meletus by asking whether anyone believes in horsemanship but not horses, or in flute-playing but not flute-players. He argues that one cannot believe in divine activities (like his daimonion) without believing in divine beings. He also argues that just as only a few trainers improve horses, few people, not everyone, improve the young.

**"The unexamined life is not worth living"**
Socrates's famous declaration at his trial in the Apology. He says he cannot stop practicing philosophy even to save his life, because questioning oneself and others is what gives life its value.

**Free meals in the Prytaneum**
When asked to propose his own penalty after conviction, Socrates ironically suggests he deserves free meals in the Prytaneum, the honor given to Olympic victors and public benefactors, because he serves the city more than any Olympian.

**Crito and the Laws of Athens**
In Plato's Crito, Socrates's wealthy friend Crito offers to help him escape from prison. Socrates refuses by imagining the personified Laws of Athens addressing him, arguing that he has an implicit agreement with the city to obey its laws, an early version of social contract theory. The dialogue opens with Socrates recounting a dream of a woman in white who tells him "on the third day you will go to fertile Phthia," a line adapted from the Iliad that predicts his death.

**Daimonion (divine sign)**
Socrates claimed that an inner divine voice or sign, his daimonion, warned him whenever he was about to do something wrong. It never told him what to do, only what not to do, and his opponents cited it as evidence that he introduced new gods.

**Meno and the slave boy (recollection)**
In Plato's Meno, Socrates questions an uneducated slave boy and leads him to discover that a square built on the diagonal of a given square has double its area. Socrates uses this to argue that learning is really anamnesis, or recollection of knowledge the soul already had.

**Socratic method, elenchus, and irony**
Socrates's method of cross-examination (elenchus) involves asking questions to expose contradictions in someone's beliefs. His habit of feigning ignorance in these debates is called Socratic irony (from the Greek eironeia). Many early dialogues are "aporetic," ending in puzzlement without a firm answer.

**Euthyphro dilemma**
In Plato's Euthyphro, Socrates questions a priest who is prosecuting his own father for murder. He asks whether something is pious because the gods love it, or whether the gods love it because it is pious, a question still central to debates about divine command ethics.

**Midwife and Diotima**
In the Theaetetus, Socrates compares himself to a midwife (his mother was one) who cannot produce ideas himself but helps others give birth to theirs. In the Symposium, he says he learned the philosophy of love from the priestess Diotima, who told him Love is the child of Poros (Resource) and Penia (Poverty).
